title: The Barium That Should Not Have Been There
paragraphs: In 1934 Enrico Fermi's group in Rome, bombarding one element after another with neutrons, reached uranium, the heaviest element then known, and found something new.

The irradiated uranium gave off radioactivities whose half-lives matched no known substance, and Fermi suggested, cautiously, that a uranium nucleus had captured a neutron and then decayed into an element beyond uranium, number 93.
The idea was reasonable: in lighter elements a captured neutron moved the nucleus at most a step or two along the periodic table.

Over the next four years laboratories in Rome, Paris, and Berlin reported a growing family of supposed transuranic elements, and Fermi's 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics credited him with new radioactive elements made by neutron irradiation.
One chemist objected almost at once.

Ida Noddack, a German chemist who had helped discover rhenium, pointed out in 1934 that Fermi had ruled out only the elements near uranium, and that the nucleus might instead have broken into several large fragments of elements far down the table.
She offered no mechanism, and physicists, who had every reason to think a nucleus could shed only a small particle at a time, set the suggestion aside.
In hindsight the paper reads as prophecy; at the time it read as a chemist straying outside her field, and I think the second reading, though wrong, was not unreasonable.

Otto Hahn, a radiochemist, and Lise Meitner, a physicist from Vienna, had worked together in Berlin since 1907, and at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Chemistry the analytical chemist Fritz Strassmann joined their uranium work in the 1930s.
Their method was the radiochemist's oldest trick: add a known element as a carrier, precipitate it out of solution, and see whether the unknown radioactivity comes down with it.

By 1938 the team had sorted the uranium products into supposed chains of transuranic elements and, separately, a few isotopes of radium, element 88, which they thought arose when the nucleus shed two alpha particles.
Then the team came apart.

Meitner was of Jewish descent, and her Austrian citizenship had shielded her from the laws that drove other Jewish scientists from German institutions; when Germany annexed Austria in March 1938, that shield vanished.
In July she slipped out of Germany with the help of the Dutch physicist Dirk Coster and settled in Stockholm, where she had a place to work but little equipment and few colleagues.
The radium was the problem.
Radium and barium occupy the same column of the periodic table and behave alike in solution, so the Berlin chemists had been using barium as the carrier for their radium isotopes.

To prove that the activity really was radium, they had to separate it from the barium, as Marie Curie had done decades earlier by fractional crystallization, which works because radium salts crystallize out of a solution slightly ahead of barium salts.

In December 1938 Hahn and Strassmann found that the separation would not work: the activity stayed with the barium through every cycle, while known radium isotopes added to the same solutions as controls separated cleanly.
Only one conclusion fit the chemistry: the product was not radium at all but barium, element 56, with barely more than half the mass of uranium.

In the paper they submitted to the journal Naturwissenschaften on December 22, they wrote that as chemists they had to call the substance barium, but that as nuclear chemists they could not yet bring themselves to a step that contradicted all previous experience of nuclear physics.
Hahn had already described the result to Meitner in a letter dated December 19 and asked whether she could think of any explanation.
She was spending Christmas in a small town on the Swedish west coast, and her nephew Otto Robert Frisch, a physicist at Niels Bohr's institute in Copenhagen, came to join her.
Frisch later recalled that they worked the problem through on a walk in the snow, he on skis and she on foot, stopping to do the arithmetic on scraps of paper.
The tool they reached for was a picture of the nucleus that Bohr had been developing in Copenhagen: the liquid drop.

In this picture the nucleus is not a rigid structure but something like a droplet of water, held together by a short-range attraction that acts like surface tension and pulled apart by the electrical repulsion among its protons.

For a small nucleus the surface tension wins easily; as the charge grows, the repulsion grows faster, and Meitner and Frisch estimated that for a nucleus with a charge of about 100 the surface tension would vanish altogether.
Uranium, with 92 protons, sits uncomfortably close to that limit.
An arriving neutron adds energy and sets the drop oscillating; it stretches, develops a waist, and, if the stretch goes far enough, snaps into two smaller drops that fly apart.
On this view barium was an expected fragment, and its partner, to bring the charges to 92, would be krypton, with 36 protons.
Two calculations clinched the argument.
The repulsion between two freshly separated fragments of roughly equal charge would drive them apart with about 200 million electron volts, far beyond anything seen in ordinary radioactive decay.

Meitner, who remembered how to compute nuclear masses from a formula then in use, asked where that energy would come from: the two fragments together weighed about one fifth of a proton mass less than the uranium nucleus and its captured neutron, and by Einstein's relation between mass and energy that missing fifth came to about 200 million electron volts.
The two numbers matched.
Back in Copenhagen in January, Frisch detected the energetic fragments directly in an ionization chamber and borrowed from a visiting biologist the word for a dividing cell: fission.
Their paper appeared in Nature in February 1939; by then Bohr, who had heard the news from Frisch before sailing, had carried it to the United States.

By September 1939 Bohr and the American physicist John Wheeler had turned the drop into a quantitative theory and argued that it was the rare isotope uranium-235, not the common uranium-238, that split when struck by a slow neutron.
What followed, the chain reaction and the weapons built on it, lies outside this account, except to note that Meitner declined to work on the bomb.
The prize came after the war.

The Nobel Prize in Chemistry for 1944, which the committee had held in reserve, was awarded in November 1945 to Hahn alone, for the discovery of the fission of heavy nuclei; he learned of it from a newspaper while interned at Farm Hall in England.
Strassmann, who had done much of the work at the bench, was not named, and neither was Meitner, though she was nominated many times for both the chemistry and the physics prize.
Hahn's own view, held to the end of his life, was that fission had been a chemical discovery, made by chemists, after the physicist had left.
I find that account true in its particulars and misleading as a whole.
It was the chemistry of Hahn and Strassmann, careful and beautifully controlled, that forced the word barium onto the page, and nothing here should diminish that.

But it was Meitner who had guided the physics of the Berlin program for years, who urged Hahn to recheck the radium, and who, with Frisch, turned an impossible result into a mechanism, a pair of fragments, and an energy.

Historians who examined the Nobel committee's records once they were opened concluded that its evaluators, chemists judging a chemical prize, underrated the interpretation and never grasped how thoroughly the work had crossed disciplinary lines.
I am wary of recasting the past as a simple tale of theft; the committee worked from the papers in front of it, in a year when little else was clear.
Still, the barium that should not have been there was discovered twice: once in a Berlin laboratory, by chemists who could not believe it, and once on a walk in the snow, by two physicists who could.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Fermi proposed in 1934 that the new radioactivities from irradiated uranium came from
choices: the splitting of a uranium nucleus into two lighter fragments of similar size
a nucleus that had captured a neutron and then decayed into element 93
isotopes of radium formed when the nucleus shed two alpha particles
a contaminant that had entered the samples during the neutron bombardment
slow neutrons that had been absorbed by lighter elements near the sample

proof.quote: a uranium nucleus had captured a neutron and then decayed into an element beyond uranium, number 93

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says Fermi suggested that a uranium nucleus had captured a neutron and then decayed into an element beyond uranium, number 93. The other choices are later ideas or ideas nobody in the passage proposed.
distractorNotes: Wrong time: splitting is the interpretation Meitner and Frisch reach in paragraphs 7 and 8, not Fermi's 1934 proposal.
Wrong group: the radium isotopes are the Berlin team's belief in paragraph 3, not Fermi's.
Outside the passage: no contamination is ever mentioned.
Mash-up: slow neutrons appear only in paragraph 9, and nothing says lighter elements absorbed them.

questions.stem: The author discusses Ida Noddack in paragraph 2 primarily to
choices: prove that chemists understood the nucleus better than physicists did
credit her with the first direct detection of fission fragments
argue that Fermi should have shared his Nobel Prize with her
show that the right idea had surfaced early and been set aside
explain the chemical method by which rhenium had been discovered

proof.quote: set the suggestion aside
In hindsight the paper reads as prophecy

questions.why: Paragraph 2 presents Noddack's 1934 suggestion that the nucleus had broken into large fragments, says physicists set it aside, and calls the paper prophecy in hindsight. She is there to show that the right idea arrived early and went unheeded.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the author also says the physicists' reading, though wrong, was not unreasonable.
Wrong person: the fragments were detected by Frisch in paragraph 8; Noddack offered no mechanism and no measurement.
Outside the passage: the author never says who should have shared Fermi's prize.
Wrong focus: rhenium is a passing credential, and the method of its discovery is never described.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Berlin group's basic method was to
choices: measure the half-life of each new radioactivity and match it to a known element
bombard a sample with slow neutrons and count the fragments in an ionization chamber
compute the masses of the products from a formula and compare them with uranium
crystallize the products repeatedly until only the heaviest element remained
add a known element as a carrier and see whether the activity followed it

proof.quote: add a known element as a carrier, precipitate it out of solution, and see whether the unknown radioactivity comes down with it

questions.why: Paragraph 3 calls it the radiochemist's oldest trick: add a known element as a carrier, precipitate it out of solution, and see whether the unknown radioactivity comes down with it.
distractorNotes: Wrong paragraph: half-lives belong to Fermi's work in paragraph 1, and the passage never says the Berlin team matched them to elements.
Wrong person: the ionization chamber is Frisch's experiment in paragraph 8.
Wrong person: computing masses from a formula is Meitner's step in paragraph 8.
Half right: fractional crystallization appears in paragraph 5, but it was used to separate radium from barium, not to isolate the heaviest element.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Meitner lost her protection from the laws aimed at Jewish scientists when
choices: Germany annexed Austria in March 1938
the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute dismissed its Jewish staff
she published the barium result with Hahn and Strassmann
Dirk Coster arrived in Berlin from the Netherlands
Hahn and Strassmann found the barium in December 1938

proof.quote: when Germany annexed Austria in March 1938, that shield vanished

questions.why: Paragraph 4 says her Austrian citizenship had shielded her, and that when Germany annexed Austria in March 1938 that shield vanished.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: no dismissal by the institute is described.
Wrong fact: she was not an author of that paper, which came five months after she left.
Reversed role: Coster helped her escape; his arrival did not change her legal standing.
Wrong time: the barium came in December 1938, well after she had fled in July.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Berlin chemists used barium as a carrier for radium because the two elements
choices: have nearly identical half-lives when they are radioactive
had been separated by Marie Curie decades earlier
occupy the same column and behave alike in solution
are both produced when a uranium nucleus sheds two alpha particles
crystallize out of a solution at exactly the same rate

proof.quote: Radium and barium occupy the same column of the periodic table and behave alike in solution

questions.why: Paragraph 5 explains that radium and barium occupy the same column of the periodic table and behave alike in solution, which is exactly what a carrier needs to do.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: no half-lives are given for either element.
Half right: Curie did separate them, but that explains why a separation was possible, not why barium was chosen as the carrier.
Wrong fact: paragraph 3 says the team thought radium arose that way; barium was the carrier they added, not a product.
Reversed: paragraph 5 says radium salts crystallize slightly ahead of barium salts, which is how the two can be told apart.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if the activity in the December 1938 solutions had really been radium, Hahn and Strassmann would have observed that
choices: the activity stayed with the barium through every cycle of crystallization
the activity crystallized out slightly ahead of the barium
the known radium isotopes added as controls failed to separate
the barium carrier lost its radioactivity as soon as it dissolved
the product weighed barely more than half as much as uranium

proof.quote: radium salts crystallize out of a solution slightly ahead of barium salts
known radium isotopes added to the same solutions as controls separated cleanly

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says radium salts crystallize slightly ahead of barium salts, and that known radium isotopes added as controls separated cleanly. Real radium would have pulled ahead of the barium; the activity never did.
distractorNotes: Reversed: that is what they actually saw, and it is the evidence that the activity was not radium.
Reversed: the controls did separate, and nothing about the unknown would change that.
Outside the passage: nothing says a carrier loses its activity on dissolving.
Wrong element: that is the mass of barium, the conclusion the chemistry forced, not a sign of radium.

questions.stem: According to the passage, all of the following are true of Hahn and Strassmann's December 1938 work EXCEPT:
choices: The activity stayed with the barium through every cycle of separation.
Known radium isotopes added as controls separated from the barium cleanly.
The paper was submitted to Naturwissenschaften on December 22.
The authors wrote that, as chemists, they were obliged to call the substance barium.
The authors concluded at once that the nucleus had split in two.

proof.quote: the activity stayed with the barium through every cycle
known radium isotopes added to the same solutions as controls separated cleanly
submitted to the journal Naturwissenschaften on December 22
as chemists they had to call the substance barium
could not yet bring themselves to a step that contradicted all previous experience of nuclear physics

questions.why: Paragraph 5 ends with the authors saying they could not yet bring themselves to a step that contradicted all previous experience of nuclear physics; the idea that the nucleus had split came from Meitner and Frisch in paragraphs 7 and 8. The other four statements are all in paragraph 5.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 5: the activity stayed with the barium through every cycle.
Stated in paragraph 5: the radium controls separated cleanly.
Stated in paragraph 5: submitted to Naturwissenschaften on December 22.
Stated in paragraph 5: as chemists they had to call the substance barium.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 7, the word 'picture' most nearly means
choices: a photograph taken with a powerful instrument
a painting of a scene from nature
a simplified model of how something behaves
an exact record of every measurement made
a vivid story told mainly to entertain

proof.quote: a picture of the nucleus that Bohr had been developing in Copenhagen: the liquid drop

questions.why: Paragraph 7 calls the liquid drop a picture of the nucleus and then describes how such a drop behaves, so the word means a model or way of thinking about the nucleus, not an actual image.
distractorNotes: The everyday meaning, but no instrument or photograph of a nucleus appears anywhere in the passage.
Another common meaning of the word that has nothing to do with the sentence.
Too strong: the liquid drop is a simplification that compares the nucleus to a droplet; it records no measurements.
Wrong register: the drop is a scientific tool used to explain a result, not entertainment.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Meitner and Frisch estimated that a nucleus would have no surface tension left once its charge reached about
choices: thirty-six
fifty-six
eighty-eight
one hundred
ninety-two

proof.quote: for a nucleus with a charge of about 100 the surface tension would vanish altogether

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says Meitner and Frisch estimated that for a nucleus with a charge of about 100 the surface tension would vanish altogether; uranium, at 92, sits close to that limit but not at it.
distractorNotes: Wrong number: 36 is krypton's proton count in paragraph 7.
Wrong number: 56 is barium's atomic number in paragraph 5.
Wrong number: 88 is radium's atomic number in paragraph 3.
Wrong number: 92 is uranium, which paragraph 7 says sits close to the limit, not at it.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that, compared with uranium, a nucleus with far fewer protons would be
choices: much less likely to split when a neutron arrives
more strongly pulled apart by electrical repulsion
unable to capture a neutron in the first place
likely to break into more than two fragments
held together by a stronger attraction between its protons

proof.quote: For a small nucleus the surface tension wins easily; as the charge grows, the repulsion grows faster
Uranium, with 92 protons, sits uncomfortably close to that limit.

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says that for a small nucleus the surface tension wins easily and that repulsion grows faster than cohesion as the charge grows. A nucleus far from the limit would hold together where uranium barely does.
distractorNotes: Reversed: repulsion grows with charge, so fewer protons means less repulsion, not more.
Too extreme: paragraph 1 says lighter elements did capture neutrons; they simply moved a step along the table.
Outside the passage: nothing links fewer protons to more fragments.
Wrong force: paragraph 7 says the protons repel one another; what holds the nucleus together is a separate short-range attraction.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the two fragments together weighed less than the uranium nucleus and its captured neutron by about
choices: the mass of one neutron
the mass of two alpha particles
one fifth of a proton mass
half the mass of uranium
200 proton masses

proof.quote: about one fifth of a proton mass less than the uranium nucleus and its captured neutron

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says the two fragments together weighed about one fifth of a proton mass less than the uranium nucleus and its captured neutron, and that this missing fifth came to about 200 million electron volts.
distractorNotes: Wrong figure: the neutron is part of what was weighed, not the amount that went missing.
Wrong paragraph: two alpha particles are the Berlin team's earlier idea about radium in paragraph 3.
Confused: barium has barely more than half the mass of uranium, but that is a fragment's mass, not the missing mass.
Confused: 200 is the energy in million electron volts, not a count of proton masses.

questions.stem: The author's remark in paragraph 8 that 'the two numbers matched' serves primarily to
choices: suggest that the agreement was too neat to be taken at face value
show that two independent calculations gave the same answer
explain why Frisch chose the word fission for the process
contrast Meitner's arithmetic with Hahn's chemistry
indicate that Bohr had already carried the news abroad

proof.quote: Two calculations clinched the argument.
The two numbers matched.

questions.why: Paragraph 8 opens by saying two calculations clinched the argument: one from the repulsion of the fragments, one from the missing mass. That the two numbers matched is what made the argument convincing.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the author presents the match as clinching the argument, not as suspicious.
Wrong detail: the word fission came from a biologist's term for a dividing cell, not from the energy calculation.
Wrong contrast: both numbers in paragraph 8 are physics calculations by Meitner and Frisch.
Wrong sentence: Bohr's trip is mentioned at the end of the paragraph and is not what the match shows.

questions.stem: Which new situation best illustrates the principle described in paragraph 7?
choices: A rubber band keeps stretching the harder it is pulled and never snaps
A boulder splits only after it is struck many times with a heavy sledgehammer
A magnet lifts more iron filings the closer it is brought to the pile
A bubble blown almost to bursting pops at a puff a small bubble survives
A sand pile grows taller and taller and never collapses under its own weight

proof.quote: For a small nucleus the surface tension wins easily
Uranium, with 92 protons, sits uncomfortably close to that limit.
An arriving neutron adds energy and sets the drop oscillating

questions.why: Paragraph 7 describes a system near its limit of stability: a small nucleus holds together easily, but uranium sits so close to the point where cohesion fails that one arriving neutron is enough to split it. A bubble near bursting that pops at a puff a small bubble survives is the same pattern.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: the principle is that past some point the system snaps, not that it stretches without limit.
Wrong mechanism: the nucleus splits from a small disturbance because it is near the limit, not from repeated heavy blows.
Unrelated: this is attraction growing with closeness, with no limit and no splitting.
Contradicted: a pile that never collapses is the opposite of a drop at the edge of stability.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that when natural uranium is exposed to slow neutrons,
choices: every nucleus in the sample eventually splits into two fragments
uranium-238 splits more readily than uranium-235 does
the fragments produced are always barium and krypton
the theory of Bohr and Wheeler fails to predict the outcome
only a minority of the nuclei are of the kind that splits

proof.quote: it was the rare isotope uranium-235, not the common uranium-238, that split when struck by a slow neutron

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says the isotope that splits under slow neutrons, uranium-235, is the rare one, while uranium-238 is the common one. So in natural uranium only a minority of nuclei are the kind that splits.
distractorNotes: Too extreme: the passage says only the rare isotope splits under slow neutrons.
Reversed: paragraph 9 names uranium-235, not 238, as the isotope that splits.
Too strong: paragraph 7 gives barium and krypton as one pairing whose charges add to 92, not the only one.
Reversed: the Bohr and Wheeler theory is what identified the isotope.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for 1944 EXCEPT:
choices: It cited the discovery of the chain reaction.
It was awarded in November 1945.
Hahn learned of it from a newspaper.
Strassmann was not named.
It had been held in reserve by the Nobel committee.

proof.quote: was awarded in November 1945
he learned of it from a newspaper
Strassmann, who had done much of the work at the bench, was not named
which the committee had held in reserve
for the discovery of the fission of heavy nuclei

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says the prize went to Hahn for the discovery of the fission of heavy nuclei. The chain reaction appears only in paragraph 9, as something that followed and lies outside the account.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 10: awarded in November 1945.
Stated in paragraph 10: he learned of it from a newspaper at Farm Hall.
Stated in paragraph 10: Strassmann was not named.
Stated in paragraph 10: the committee had held it in reserve.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward Hahn's claim that fission was a chemical discovery is best described as
choices: openly contemptuous
appreciative but unconvinced
wholly persuaded by it
coolly indifferent to it
resentful on Meitner's behalf

proof.quote: I find that account true in its particulars and misleading as a whole.
careful and beautifully controlled
I am wary of recasting the past as a simple tale of theft

questions.why: Paragraph 11 calls Hahn's account true in its particulars and misleading as a whole, praises the chemistry as careful and beautifully controlled, and refuses to call the episode a theft. That is appreciation paired with disagreement.
distractorNotes: Too strong: the author praises the chemistry and says nothing should diminish it.
Reversed: the author calls the account misleading as a whole.
Too weak: the author takes a clear position and argues it across a full paragraph.
Too strong: the author says plainly that they are wary of recasting the past as a tale of theft.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Ida Noddack deserves to be remembered as the true discoverer of nuclear fission because she proposed the idea first
The liquid-drop model of the nucleus was the most important theoretical advance in physics during the 1930s
The chemistry of Hahn and Strassmann was so badly flawed that physicists had to step in and rescue the result
Fission was found by chemists who could not believe their result and explained by physicists the prize left out
The Nobel committee acted in bad faith when it gave the 1944 chemistry prize to Hahn alone and not to Meitner

proof.quote: could not yet bring themselves to a step
true in its particulars and misleading as a whole
the barium that should not have been there was discovered twice

questions.why: The passage follows the barium from the Berlin bench to the walk in the snow and closes by saying the discovery happened twice, once by chemists who could not believe it and once by physicists who could, while the prize recognized only the first. That is the whole arc.
distractorNotes: Too strong: paragraph 2 calls Noddack's idea prophecy but also says it offered no mechanism and was reasonably set aside.
Too narrow: the liquid drop is the tool of paragraph 7, and the passage never ranks it against other advances.
Reversed: paragraph 11 calls the chemistry careful and beautifully controlled.
Too strong: paragraph 11 says the author is wary of calling the episode a theft and notes the committee worked from the papers in front of it.
